questions.q: How much playing time does a game last?
questions.a: 60 minutes, in two 30-minute periods
questions.why: A game lasts for 60 minutes of play, divided into two 30-minute periods with a halftime between them.

questions.q: What is the maximum length of a Jam?
questions.a: 2 minutes
questions.why: A Jam can last up to two minutes. It may be called off earlier, for example by the Lead Jammer.

questions.q: What is the minimum time that must elapse between two Jams?
questions.a: 30 seconds
questions.why: At least 30 seconds must elapse between Jams. More than 30 seconds may not elapse unless a timeout is called.

questions.q: Which signal starts a Jam?
questions.a: A single short whistle blast
questions.why: Each Jam starts with a single short whistle blast, and finishes at the end of a series of four short whistle blasts.

questions.q: Which signal ends a Jam?
questions.a: A series of four short whistle blasts
questions.why: A Jam finishes at the end of a series of four short whistle blasts. Two short blasts indicate the Lead Jammer.

questions.q: The period clock reaches zero while a Jam is in progress. What happens?
questions.a: The period ends at the conclusion of the current Jam
w: The Jam is cancelled and replayed
An Overtime Jam is automatically played
questions.why: If the period clock reaches zero before the next Jam has started, the period ends at that moment; otherwise, the period ends at the conclusion of the final Jam for the period.

questions.q: The period clock reaches zero during the Lineup Time, before the next Jam starts. What happens?
questions.a: The period ends at that moment
w: One last Jam is played anyway
Teams have 30 seconds to request an extra Jam
The period continues until one team leads by 10 points
questions.why: If the period clock reaches zero before the next Jam has started, the period ends at that moment (barring the special cases for additional Jams).

questions.q: How many Team Timeouts can each team take during a game?
questions.a: Three per game
questions.why: Each team is given three Team Timeouts per game.

questions.q: How long is a Team Timeout?
questions.a: 60 seconds
questions.why: Team Timeouts are 60 seconds long.

questions.q: Who can call a Team Timeout?
questions.a: The team’s Captain or Alternate
w: Any staff member on the bench
questions.why: Team Timeouts may only be called by the team’s Captain or Alternate.

questions.q: The Captain is seated in the Penalty Box. Can they call a Team Timeout?
questions.a: No, a Captain serving a penalty cannot call one
w: Yes, but only during a Jam
Yes, if they stand for their last 10 seconds
questions.why: Captains or Alternates currently serving a penalty cannot call Team Timeouts (or request an Official Review).

questions.q: How many Official Reviews does a team have?
questions.a: One at the start of each period
w: Only one for the whole game
questions.why: Both teams begin each period with one Official Review which they may use during that period.

questions.q: After an Official Review, the Head Referee determines that an officiating error was made. What is the outcome for the team that requested it?
questions.a: It retains the privilege to call another review later in the period (only once per period)
w: It gains an extra Team Timeout
The opposing team loses its Official Review
It is awarded 4 points in compensation
questions.why: If an officiating error was made, the team retains the privilege to call an additional review later in the same period. The review can be retained in this manner only once per period.

questions.q: A team did not use its Official Review during the first period. What happens to it?
questions.a: It is lost: reviews are not carried forward to the next period
w: It is added to the one for the second period
It is given to the opposing team
questions.why: Official Reviews (whether unused or retained) are not carried forward to the subsequent period.

questions.q: Can a team use its Official Review as a timeout?
questions.a: Yes, as a 60-second timeout, but the review is then not retained
w: Yes, but only at the end of the game
Yes, and it can then be used again as a review
questions.why: A team may elect to use any of their Official Reviews as a 60-second timeout. In this case, the review will not be retained.

questions.q: Which officiating decisions can be the subject of an Official Review?
questions.a: Those made during the prior Jam, after it, or during the Lineup Time preceding it
w: Any decision in the current period
Only decisions made in the current Jam
questions.why: The only decisions that can be reviewed are those made during the prior Jam, after the prior Jam, or during the Lineup Time preceding the prior Jam.

questions.q: How is the end of a timeout signaled?
questions.a: With a long rolling whistle
w: With a hand signal, no whistle
questions.why: The beginning of a timeout is marked by four short whistle blasts, and the end of a timeout by a long rolling whistle.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the minimum game information that must be displayed?
questions.a: Each Skater’s penalty count
questions.why: Displayed game information must include, at a minimum, the period clock, the Jam clock and the official score. Penalty counts must be available on request (Section 5.1.2), not necessarily displayed.

questions.q: The game ends with the score tied. Which statement about the Overtime Jam is true?
questions.a: No Lead Jammer is declared
w: The Lineup Time before it is 30 seconds
Only teams with a Team Timeout left may take part
questions.why: In Overtime: the Lineup Time before the Jam is sixty seconds, no Lead Jammer is declared, and both Jammers begin scoring on their first trip through the Pack.

questions.q: During an Overtime Jam, when can Jammers start scoring points?
questions.a: On their first trip through the Pack
w: From their second trip, as usual
Only during the last minute of the Jam
questions.why: In Overtime, both Jammers begin scoring on their first trip through the Pack.

questions.q: How long is the Lineup Time before an Overtime Jam?
questions.a: 60 seconds
questions.why: The Lineup Time before an Overtime Jam is sixty seconds.

questions.q: A Jam is called off because a Skater is injured. When can they return to play?
questions.a: After sitting out the following three Jams, if they are no longer apparently injured
questions.why: A Skater whose injury alters the flow of the game may not participate during the following three Jams.

questions.q: For the second time in a period, a Skater’s injury alters the flow of the game. What is the consequence?
questions.a: They may not skate for the rest of that period
w: They are expelled from the game
They sit out another three Jams
Their team loses a Team Timeout
questions.why: A Skater whose injury alters the flow of the game more than once in a period may not participate as a Skater for the rest of that period.

questions.q: Which type of skates is allowed?
questions.a: Quad-style roller skates only
questions.why: Skaters must wear quad-style roller skates. Inline skates are not permitted.

questions.q: When may the Head Referee declare that a team has forfeited?
questions.a: If it has five or fewer Skaters eligible to participate
w: If it has fewer than eight Skaters left
questions.why: The Head Referee may declare a forfeit if a team has five or fewer Skaters eligible to participate, or refuses to field Skaters on the track.

questions.q: How must the Alternate be identified?
questions.a: By a visible “A” on their uniform or body
w: They do not need to be identified
questions.why: The Captain and Alternate must be visibly identified by wearing a “C” and an “A”, respectively, on their uniform or body.

questions.q: Does a team’s Alternate have to be a Skater?
questions.a: No, it may be a teammate, coach or manager
w: Yes, they must be on the roster
Yes, they must be the Pivot
No, but they must be an Official
questions.why: The Alternate may be a teammate, coach or manager. A team may only have one Alternate.

questions.q: Where must Skaters’ roster numbers be displayed?
questions.a: Clearly on the back and upper arm
w: On the front of the jersey only
questions.why: Roster numbers must be clearly displayed on a Skater’s back and upper arm areas.

questions.q: When can teams call a timeout?
questions.a: Only between Jams
w: At any time, even during a Jam
Only during the last minute of the period
Only after a Jam in which they scored
questions.why: Timeouts may only be called between Jams, though Officials may end a Jam in order to call an Official Timeout.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of Skaters a team can field for a Jam?
questions.a: One Jammer and at most four Blockers (one of whom may be the Pivot)
w: One Jammer, one Pivot and four Blockers
questions.why: For each Jam, a team must field one Jammer and at most four Blockers. One of these Blockers may be designated as the Pivot.

questions.q: What makes a Skater their team’s Jammer?
questions.a: Being in visible possession of the Star at the beginning of the Jam
w: Lining up behind the Jammer Line
Being named by the Captain to the referees
Being the first to get through the Pack
questions.why: The Jammer is denoted as the Skater in visible possession of the Jammer helmet cover (a.k.a. the Star) at the beginning of the Jam.

questions.q: As the Jam starts, Red 34 is behind the Jammer Line without the Star, and Red 27 is ahead of the Jammer Line with the Star. Who is the Jammer?
questions.a: Red 27, and both Skaters are penalized for their starting position
w: Red 34, because they are correctly positioned
questions.why: The Star determines who the Jammer is: Red 27. Both Skaters started the Jam entirely out of their starting location and are penalized.

questions.q: What is the Pivot’s helmet cover called?
questions.a: The Stripe
questions.why: The Pivot helmet cover, which has one long stripe down the middle of it, is called the Stripe. The Jammer helmet cover is called the Star.

questions.q: Who is allowed to control a team’s Star?
questions.a: That team’s Jammer and Pivot
questions.why: The Star may only be carried by the Jammer wearing it on their helmet, or by that team’s Jammer or Pivot holding it in their grasp. Other Skaters may not control the Star.

questions.q: How is it signaled that a Jammer has become Lead Jammer?
questions.a: With two short whistle blasts
questions.why: When one Jammer is determined to be the Lead Jammer, this is indicated by two short whistle blasts.

questions.q: How does a Jammer earn Lead Jammer status?
questions.a: By being the first eligible Jammer to pass the foremost in-play Blocker, having already passed all the other Blockers
w: By completing the first full lap of the track
By scoring the first point of the Jam
By being the first to leave the Jammer Line
questions.why: The Lead Jammer is the first eligible Jammer who establishes superior position to the foremost in-play Blocker, having already earned a pass on all Blockers (excluding those ahead of the Engagement Zone).

questions.q: The Lead Jammer’s Star falls off in normal gameplay. What happens?
questions.a: They remain Lead Jammer
w: Lead passes to the opposing Jammer
questions.why: Lead Jammer status is retained if the Star is removed in the natural course of gameplay or is removed by an opponent.

questions.q: Which of these situations makes a Jammer lose the ability to earn Lead?
questions.a: Exiting the front of the Engagement Zone without having earned Lead
w: Being passed by the opposing Jammer
questions.why: A Jammer loses the ability to earn Lead if they commit a penalty, exit the front of the Engagement Zone without having earned Lead, remove their helmet cover, or have it removed by a teammate.

questions.q: A Jammer is penalized during the Lineup Time. Can they earn Lead in the next Jam?
questions.a: No, a penalty during the preceding Lineup Time makes them ineligible for Lead
w: Yes, the penalty only counts for the previous Jam
Yes, if they leave the Penalty Box before the other Jammer
Yes, if their team uses an Official Review
questions.why: A Jammer loses the ability to earn Lead if they commit a penalty during that Jam or during the Lineup Time preceding it.

questions.q: A Pivot receives the Star through a legal Star Pass. Can they become Lead Jammer?
questions.a: No, only Skaters who start the Jam as Jammers can earn Lead
w: Yes, but only if Lead has not yet been awarded
Yes, they automatically take over Lead
questions.why: Only Skaters who start the Jam as Jammers may earn Lead: a Pivot who receives the Star cannot become Lead.

questions.q: How does the Lead Jammer call off the Jam?
questions.a: By repeatedly placing their hands on their hips
questions.why: The Lead Jammer calls off the Jam by repeatedly placing their hands on their hips.

questions.q: The Lead Jammer has lost their Star during play. Can they still call off the Jam?
questions.a: Yes, they retain the ability to call off the Jam
w: No, they must put the Star back on first
No, only the Pivot can then call it off
Yes, but only after 1 minute of the Jam
questions.why: The Lead Jammer retains the ability to call off the Jam even if they are no longer wearing the Star.

questions.q: Which Skater can call off a Jam before the two minutes have elapsed?
questions.a: Only the Lead Jammer
questions.why: The Lead Jammer is the only Skater who may end a Jam before the two minutes elapse.

questions.q: Which of these Star Passes is legal?
questions.a: The Jammer hands the Star directly to the Pivot, both upright, In Bounds and in play
w: The Jammer throws the Star to the Pivot, who catches it in the air
The Jammer gives the Star to a Non-Pivot Blocker
The Jammer gives the Star to the Pivot, who is Out of Bounds
questions.why: A legal Star Pass is a hand-to-hand transfer of the Star to the team’s Pivot, while both Skaters are upright, In Bounds, in play, and not en route to or in queue for the Penalty Box.

questions.q: After a legal Star Pass, what does the former Jammer become?
questions.a: A Non-Pivot Blocker
w: They remain a Jammer without the Star
questions.why: The previous Jammer becomes a Non-Pivot Blocker. The Pivot Role cannot be transferred during a Jam.

questions.q: After a legal Star Pass, the new Jammer…
questions.a: inherits the former Jammer’s points, current trip and passes
w: starts a fresh initial trip from zero
can no longer score points in this Jam
must get back behind the Pack before scoring
questions.why: The new Jammer inherits the previous Jammer’s points earned, trips through the Pack and Skaters passed.

questions.q: How many times can the Jammer Role be transferred by a Star Pass during a single Jam?
questions.a: Only once
w: Never during the first minute, freely afterwards
questions.why: The Jammer Role may be transferred to the Pivot once per Jam via a Star Pass. The Pivot Role cannot be transferred during a Jam.

questions.q: The Pivot’s Stripe fell off during play. The Jammer hands them the Star anyway. What happens?
questions.a: The pass is not successful: both keep their Roles and the Pivot is warned to drop the Star
w: The pass is valid and the Pivot becomes the Jammer
questions.why: A Pivot who is not wearing their helmet cover with the Stripe visible cannot receive a Star Pass. Since the Stripe fell off in normal play, they are warned and must drop the Star.

questions.q: Can a legal Star Pass be made by throwing the Star to the Pivot?
questions.a: No: a throw is an incomplete pass; a legal transfer must be hand to hand
w: Yes, if the Pivot catches it before it touches the ground
Yes, if the throw is under 10 feet
No, and it is always a penalty
questions.why: Throwing the Star is treated as an incomplete Star Pass, not an illegal one: a Star Pass cannot be legally completed by throwing it.

questions.q: White Jammer hands the Star to a Non-Pivot Blocker, who immediately drops it. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty, as there was no impact on the game
questions.why: The Jammer may only pass the Star to their Pivot, but since the Blocker immediately dropped it there was no impact. Had they not dropped it immediately, the Jammer would be penalized.

questions.q: Where must Blockers line up at the start of a Jam?
questions.a: Behind the Pivot Line and ahead of the Jammer Line
questions.why: Blockers must be behind the Pivot Line and ahead of the Jammer Line. Additionally, Pivots may be touching the Pivot Line.

questions.q: Where must Jammers line up at the start of a Jam?
questions.a: Behind or touching the Jammer Line
w: Between the Pivot Line and the Jammer Line
questions.why: Jammers must be behind or touching the Jammer Line.

questions.q: A Pivot is touching the Pivot Line at the start of the Jam. Where must the Non-Pivot Blockers be?
questions.a: Behind that Pivot
w: At least 10 feet behind that Pivot
On the Pivot Line, next to that Pivot
It makes no difference to their position
questions.why: If either Pivot is touching the Pivot Line, all non-Pivot Blockers must be behind that Pivot. A non-Pivot Blocker whose hips are ahead of that Pivot’s has committed a False Start.

questions.q: Which of these is a False Start for a Jammer?
questions.a: Gaining speed in the counterclockwise direction at the Jam start
w: Standing still while touching the Jammer Line
questions.why: A Jammer who is gaining speed in the counterclockwise direction at the Jam start has committed a False Start and must yield their position.

questions.q: As the Jam-Starting Whistle sounds, White Pivot has lined up entirely in front of the Pivot Line. What is the call?
questions.a: An immediate penalty for illegal positioning
w: A False Start warning: they must yield their position
No penalty, Pivots may be past the line
They are sent back to the bench for this Jam
questions.why: The Pivot is entirely out of their starting location: this is a flagrant violation, penalized immediately rather than with a warning.

questions.q: As the whistle sounds, Red Jammer’s skate has rolled past the Jammer Line (touching both inside and outside their starting location). What should the referee do?
questions.a: Treat it as a False Start: they must yield their position, or be penalized
w: Stop the Jam and restart it
questions.why: Touching both inside and outside your starting location is a False Start: the Skater must yield, and is penalized only if they fail to do so.

questions.q: As the Jam-Starting Whistle sounds, a White Blocker is Out of Bounds on the inside of the track. What happens?
questions.a: They are not on the track at the start of the Jam: they return to the bench and do not take part in this Jam
w: They receive a False Start penalty
They just have to re-enter behind the Pack
questions.why: Any Skater who is not fully on the track at the Jam-Starting Whistle does not take part in the Jam. Even straddling the boundary, they would be considered Out of Bounds.

questions.q: At the start of a Jam, the previous Jam’s Jammer is still seated in the Penalty Box. Who is their team’s Jammer for this Jam?
questions.a: That same Skater, still in the Penalty Box
w: The Skater wearing the Star on the Jammer Line
The team plays without a Jammer
questions.why: The order for identifying the Jammer is: 1. the previous Jam’s Jammer who is in, or en route to, the Penalty Box; 2. the Skater controlling the Star in the Jammer Starting Position; 3. the Skater controlling the Star In Bounds but out of position.

questions.q: Which of these privileges does NOT belong to the Pivot?
questions.a: Scoring points by passing opponents
w: Becoming the Jammer through a Star Pass
Controlling the Star (picking it up, moving it)
Starting the Jam touching the Pivot Line
questions.why: The Pivot is a Blocker: they do not score points unless they become the Jammer. Their privileges: becoming the Jammer, controlling the Star and touching the Pivot Line at the start.

questions.q: Can a team start a Jam without any Blocker who is not serving a penalty?
questions.a: No, it must field at least one Blocker who is not serving a penalty
w: Yes, if its Jammer is on the track
Yes, if its Pivot is in the Penalty Box
Yes, it is an allowed tactical choice
questions.why: Teams must field at least one Blocker who is not serving a penalty.

questions.q: A Blocker jumps from out of bounds to reach the track and is still airborne when the Jam-Starting Whistle sounds. What happens?
questions.a: They are considered Out of Bounds: they return to the bench and do not take part in the Jam
w: They take part in the Jam normally
They receive a False Start warning
They must get behind the Pack
questions.why: While airborne, a Skater retains the status they had before (here, Out of Bounds). So they were not on the track at the start of the Jam.

questions.q: Red Jammer tucks the Star into their jersey to have their hands free while going through the Pack. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty: they are concealing their Jammer Role
w: They simply lose the right to score
questions.why: The Jammer and Pivot may not hide the Star. Concealing one’s Role is unsporting. Holding the Star visibly in their hand would not have been penalized.

questions.q: How is the Pack defined?
questions.a: The largest group of Blockers in proximity, upright and In Bounds, containing members of both teams
w: The group of Skaters, Jammers included, around the Pivot
All the Blockers on the track
The foremost group of Blockers on the track
questions.why: The Pack is the largest group of Blockers in proximity, skating upright and In Bounds, containing members from both teams. Jammers are not part of this definition.

questions.q: What maximum distance defines “proximity” between Pack Blockers?
questions.why: Proximity is defined as not more than 10 feet (3.05 m) in front of or behind the nearest Pack Skater.

questions.q: How far does the Engagement Zone extend?
questions.a: Up to 20 feet (6.10 m) ahead of the foremost and behind the rearmost Pack Skaters
w: Up to 10 feet (3.05 m) ahead of and behind the Pack
Along the whole straightaway where the Pack is
Up to 10 m ahead of the Pack only
questions.why: The Engagement Zone extends 20 feet (6.10 m) ahead of the foremost Pack Skater and 20 feet behind the rearmost Pack Skater.

questions.q: How are distances measured to determine the Pack and the Engagement Zone?
questions.a: Between Skaters’ hips, parallel to the inside track boundary
w: In a straight line from shoulder to shoulder
questions.why: Distances are measured as the shortest distance, parallel to the inside track boundary, between Skaters’ hips.

questions.q: There are two groups of Blockers of the same size, more than 10 feet apart. Where is the Pack?
questions.a: There is no Pack (No Pack)
w: It is the group with the most Pivots
It is the group closest to the Jammers
questions.why: If no single group of Blockers meets the definition, there is no Pack, even if there are multiple groups of the same size.

questions.q: Can a group made up only of Red Blockers be the Pack?
questions.a: No, the Pack must contain members from both teams
w: Yes, if it is the largest group
Yes, if the Red Pivot is part of it
Yes, but only on the straightaway
questions.why: The Pack must contain Blockers from both teams.

questions.q: When is a Blocker “Out of Play”?
questions.a: When they are In Bounds but outside the Engagement Zone
w: When they are Out of Bounds
questions.why: A Blocker is Out of Play when they are In Bounds but positioned outside of the Engagement Zone. When there is No Pack, all Blockers are Out of Play.

questions.q: In a No Pack situation, which Blockers are Out of Play?
questions.a: All Blockers
w: Only those in the front group
Only those who caused the No Pack
questions.why: When there is No Pack, all Blockers are Out of Play: they can neither engage nor be engaged.

questions.q: During a No Pack, what must a Blocker in the front group do?
questions.a: Actively brake until they come to a complete stop, without being required to skate clockwise
w: Skate clockwise back to the rear group
questions.why: If a Blocker is in the front group, they must actively brake until they come to a complete stop (coasting is insufficient), but they are not required to skate clockwise.

questions.q: During a No Pack, what must a Blocker in the rear group do?
questions.a: Accelerate (until sprinting) toward the front group until a Pack is reformed
w: Coast while waiting for the front group
questions.why: The rear group must accelerate until a Pack is reformed. Coasting or stepping slowly is insufficient. They may slow to avoid unsafe contact when Pack reformation is imminent.

questions.q: A Blocker blocks an opponent with impact while there is No Pack. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty: blocks with impact while there is no Pack should be penalized
w: No penalty if the block uses legal zones
No penalty if they are in the rear group
questions.why: Blocks on or by Blockers which have impact while there is no Pack should be penalized.

questions.q: A Blocker is ahead of the Engagement Zone and is warned. The Pack is moving counterclockwise. Must they skate clockwise to return?
questions.a: No: they must immediately attempt to return, but only have to skate clockwise if the Pack is stopped or moving clockwise
w: No, they may stay ahead as long as they block nobody
Yes, and they must also come to a full stop
questions.why: Warned Blockers must immediately attempt to return to the Engagement Zone. Those ahead of it are only compelled to skate clockwise if the Pack is stopped or moving clockwise.

questions.q: A Blocker has just been penalized but is still physically on the track. Do they count for Pack definition?
questions.a: No, a penalized Skater is considered no longer on the track for Pack definition
w: Yes, until they leave the track
Only if they are the Pivot
questions.why: When a Skater is penalized, they are considered to no longer be on the track for the purposes of Pack definition and relative position.

questions.q: The Red wall skates forward slowly while the White Blockers stand still, until a No Pack results. What is the call?
questions.a: No Pack is declared, no penalty
w: Penalty to the Red Blockers for destroying the Pack
questions.why: By skating slowly, Red gave White the opportunity to maintain the Pack: no penalty. However, had White skated clockwise or taken a knee, they would have been penalized.

questions.q: At the whistle, the Red Blockers stay still while the White Blockers skate counterclockwise, creating a No Pack. What is the call?
questions.a: No Pack, no penalty for destroying the Pack (neither team changed speed)
w: Penalty to Red, for standing still
Penalty to White, for starting too fast
questions.why: A Pack destruction penalty requires a team that is clearly responsible, typically the one that changes its speed relative to the established speed of the Pack. Here nobody changed speed. Both teams must then reform the Pack.

questions.q: Red Pivot, the only Red Blocker on the track, intentionally skates Out of Bounds. What is the call?
questions.a: No Pack, and Red Pivot is penalized (they must stay on the track)
questions.why: Their illegal action destroyed the Pack. As the last Red Blocker, they must stay on the track so that a Pack can exist.

questions.q: Red Pivot, who links the two groups, leaves the track because their knee pad slipped, creating a No Pack. What is the call?
questions.a: No Pack, no penalty: they acted to address a safety issue
w: The Jam is stopped for injury
questions.why: Skaters are not penalized when they act to address a safety concern.

questions.q: Can a Jammer exit and remain outside the Engagement Zone?
questions.a: Yes, it is a Jammer privilege
w: No, they would be Out of Play
Yes, but only if they are Lead Jammer
No, except to go to the Penalty Box
questions.why: Jammers may legally exit and remain outside of the Engagement Zone. They are not part of the Pack definition.

questions.q: No Pack: the White Blockers in front keep blocking Red Jammer without trying to reform the Pack, and the Red Blockers behind stay stopped for a few seconds. Who is penalized?
questions.a: One White Blocker and one Red Blocker
w: Nobody, reforming the Pack is the referees’ job
questions.why: All Blockers must try to reform the Pack. Only one Blocker per responsible team is penalized (and again if the Pack is still not reformed).

questions.q: The Pack is stopped. A Blocker skates clockwise until the Pack is destroyed. Is this legal?
questions.a: No, it is illegal
w: Yes, clockwise skating is always allowed
Yes, if they are the Pivot
Yes, if they stay In Bounds
questions.why: When the Pack is moving counterclockwise, stopped, or has no established speed, clockwise skating which destroys the Pack is illegal.

questions.q: A Red Blocker legally blocks a White Blocker Out of Bounds. No White Blocker is now within 10 feet of a Red one. What happens?
questions.a: No Pack, no penalty: White must return as soon as possible and Red must skate counterclockwise to let them back in
w: Pack destruction penalty to the Red Blocker
The Pack is formed by the Red Blockers alone
questions.why: Without a White Blocker in proximity to a Red one, no Pack can be defined. Everyone must work to reform it. The destruction resulted from normal gameplay and is not penalized.

questions.q: Which of these parts of an opponent’s body is a Legal Target Zone?
questions.a: The arms and hands
questions.why: It is only legal to initiate a block to an opponent’s chest, front and sides of the torso, arms, hands, hips, and the front and sides of the legs above mid-thigh.

questions.q: Which parts of your body can you legally initiate a block with?
questions.a: The torso, arms above the elbow and legs above mid-thigh
w: The torso, whole arms and hands
Any part covered by protective gear
questions.why: It is only legal to initiate a block using the torso, arms above the elbow, and legs above mid-thigh.

questions.q: Are an opponent’s buttocks and the back of their thighs a Legal Target Zone?
questions.a: No, the back of the body (including the buttocks and back of the thighs) is an Illegal Target Zone
w: Yes, if the contact is light
questions.why: Illegal Target Zones include the back of the body (including the back of the buttocks and thighs), the head down to the collarbone, and the legs from below mid-thigh to the wheels.

questions.q: This diagram shows the Legal Blocking Zones. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.a: The forearm and hand
questions.why: Illegal Blocking Zones include the head, the forearm (from the point of the elbow to the fingertips) and the legs below mid-thigh.

questions.q: A Jammer initiates a block with their forearms tucked into their torso, to a Legal Target Zone. The opponent falls Out of Bounds. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: forearms tucked into the torso are a Legal Blocking Zone
w: Penalty only because the opponent went out
questions.why: Forearms are considered a Legal Blocking Zone when they are held tucked into the initiator’s torso.

questions.q: Which contact should be penalized regardless of impact?
questions.a: Avoidable forceful contact to the back, or any forceful contact to the head or neck
w: Any contact that makes the opponent fall
questions.why: For safety reasons, avoidable forceful contact to the back, or any forceful contact to the head or neck, should be penalized regardless of impact.

questions.q: A legal chest-to-chest block causes forceful secondary contact of the arm to the opponent’s neck; their head jerks back, but they neither fall nor lose position. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for the initiator
w: No penalty, as no position was lost
No penalty, as the initial block was legal
questions.why: Even if the initial block is legal and no position is lost, forceful contact to the head or neck should always result in a penalty. Non-forceful incidental contact without impact would not be penalized.

questions.q: Is a counter-block considered a block?
questions.a: Yes, it follows the same rules as a block
w: No, it is always a legal defensive action
Only if it knocks the opponent down
questions.why: Counter-blocking is movement toward an oncoming block in order to counter an opponent’s block. A counter-block is a block.

questions.q: Which of these Skaters can legally initiate a block?
questions.a: An upright, in-play, In Bounds Blocker skating counterclockwise
w: A Blocker standing still on their toe stops
A Blocker who is Out of Bounds
questions.why: Skaters may not initiate a block while Down, Out of Bounds, Out of Play, airborne, stopped, or skating clockwise.

questions.q: Can you initiate a block on an opponent who is straddling the track boundary?
questions.a: Yes
w: No, they are considered Out of Bounds
Only if they are a Jammer
questions.why: Skaters may initiate a block on someone who is straddling the track boundary, stopped, or moving in any direction.

questions.q: A Red Blocker legally pushes a White Blocker until they are completely Out of Bounds, then initiates a new block that knocks them down. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for the Red Blocker
w: No penalty, it is part of the same block
Penalty for the White Blocker who went out
questions.why: It is only legal to block a Skater who is In Bounds or straddling the line. The new block on a fully Out of Bounds opponent warrants the penalty.

questions.q: A Blocker helps a Down teammate get back up. Is this legal?
questions.a: Yes, it is allowed
w: No, you may not assist a Down teammate
Only if both are Out of Play
questions.why: You may not assist a teammate who is Down, Out of Play or Out of Bounds, but it is legal to help a Down teammate get back up.

questions.q: Two Red Blockers link arms to form a wall. White Pivot tries to get between them and fails. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for the Blocker most responsible for the link
w: No penalty, walls are a legal tactic
questions.why: Forming a wall by linking or grasping teammates is illegal if an opponent attempts to pass and fails because of it. If it is unclear who initiated the link, the one closest to the referee is penalized.

questions.q: White Pivot, standing still on their toe stops, blocks Red Jammer and stops them completely. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for White Pivot, because they were stopped
w: No penalty, using toe stops is legal
Penalty for Red Jammer for counter-blocking
questions.why: Actively maintaining a stopped position that impedes an opponent is penalized. Toe stops are not the issue: had they kept moving counterclockwise on their toe stops, there would be no penalty.

questions.q: Before the Jam-Starting Whistle, Red Jammer knocks White Jammer Out of Bounds to take their spot. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for Red, who also loses Lead eligibility; White may take part in the Jam
w: No penalty, the Jam has not started
White cannot take part in the Jam because they were Out of Bounds
The Jam is delayed and restarted
questions.why: Blocking before a Jam starts is illegal. Since White is out of position due to an opponent’s illegal action, they may take part in the Jam.

questions.q: A Blocker initiates contact during the Jam-Ending Whistle; the opponent loses balance just after the Jam ends. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: the block was legally initiated before the Jam ended
w: Penalty: blocking during the ending whistles is illegal
Penalty only if the opponent falls
A warning for play after the Jam
questions.why: Blocking after the Jam has ended is illegal, but it is legal to initiate during the Jam-Ending Whistle, even if the result happens afterwards.

questions.q: Stuck behind a wall, White Jammer intentionally and forcefully knees a Red Blocker in the buttocks, without getting through. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty, regardless of loss of position
w: No penalty, since they gained no position
Penalty only if the Blocker falls
questions.why: An intentional, forceful elbow or knee is dangerous and unsporting: it is penalized regardless of any advantage gained.

questions.q: A White Blocker intentionally falls on top of a crouching Red Blocker, targeting a Legal Target Zone. What is the call?
questions.a: Expulsion for Unsporting Conduct
w: No penalty, the target zone is legal
Penalty for the crouching Red Blocker
questions.why: Intentionally falling onto an opponent is extremely dangerous and unsporting. Skaters accidentally falling on each other due to natural gameplay are not concerned.

questions.q: After contact, a Blocker “falls small” (arms and legs tucked in) and an opponent trips over them. It is the first time. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty
w: Penalty for the Skater who fell
Penalty for the opponent who tripped
questions.why: Falling small is what is expected to limit the danger. Only if it happened repeatedly (for example, a third time) should it be penalized.

questions.q: A Red Blocker blocks White Pivot, who falls onto a teammate already Down right in front of them. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for the Red Blocker
w: No penalty if the block was legal
questions.why: Blocking a Skater onto or over a Down Skater is dangerous. Had the block been initiated before the other Skater fell, there would have been no penalty.

questions.q: A Blocker is knocked off balance and grabs an opponent’s jersey to regain it, slowing the opponent considerably. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty: they used an Illegal Blocking Zone with impact
w: No penalty, the opponent did not fall
questions.why: Assists taken from an opponent (whips, braces…) are penalized if they give an advantage to the initiator or a disadvantage to the opponent.

questions.q: A very forceful but entirely legal block (legal zones, in play) injures an opponent. The opposing Captain asks for an expulsion. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: you cannot be expelled for legal play
questions.why: The rules clearly state how to block, and the block met every standard. A Skater cannot be expelled for legal play.

questions.q: Jumping to pass, Red Jammer, fully airborne, unintentionally hits a Blocker, who is knocked out of their position in the wall. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for Red Jammer
w: No penalty, the contact was unintentional
questions.why: Initiating a block while fully airborne is dangerous. Here the Blocker lost their established position. Light contact without impact would not have been penalized.

questions.q: A legal block deflects Red Jammer, who unavoidably crashes into the back of another opposing Blocker. That Blocker does not lose position. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: the contact was unavoidable and had no further consequence
w: Penalty: any forceful contact to the back is penalized
Penalty for the Blocker who deflected the Jammer
questions.why: The illegal contact resulted from an opponent’s block: it was unavoidable. Without loss of position, it does not warrant a penalty. Had the Blocker lost position, the Jammer would have been penalized.

questions.q: A Blocker traps the opposing Jammer’s shoulder between their upper arm and body and exerts constant downward force. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty: holding an opponent is not a legal form of blocking
w: No penalty if legal zones are used
No penalty, it is positional blocking
questions.why: Legal forms of blocking do not include holding an opponent, even with legal zones. Rapidly applying their entire body weight downwards would warrant an expulsion.

questions.q: Illegal contact allows a Skater to gain position on an opponent. Is that enough impact for a penalty?
questions.a: Yes, gaining or maintaining position through illegal contact always has sufficient impact
w: No, only if the opponent falls
No, only if points are scored
Only if it is a Jammer
questions.why: Gaining or maintaining superior position on an opponent through illegal contact is always considered to have sufficient impact on the game.

questions.q: Well before impact, a Blocker turns and presents their back. The opposing Jammer makes contact anyway and knocks them down. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for the Jammer, who was responsible for their block
w: Penalty for the Blocker who presented their back
questions.why: The Blocker established their new position before contact. Had they presented their back at the last moment, leaving no chance to avoid contact, they would be considered the initiator.

questions.q: The foremost Blocker faces the Jammer with arms extended and stops them with the whole arm (upper arm, elbow, forearm). The Jammer does not fall. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty: the Jammer’s progress was impeded with Illegal Blocking Zones
w: No penalty, no position was lost
No penalty, the upper arm is legal
questions.why: It is the sustained impact of the forearm and elbow that makes this penalizable. Had the Blocker dropped their forearm as soon as contact was made, there would have been no penalty.

questions.q: How does a Jammer score a point?
questions.a: By lapping an opposing Blocker (passing them twice in a row), with an earned pass
w: For every full lap of the track
For every opponent passed, Jammer included
Every time they leave the Pack
questions.why: Jammers score a point each time they lap an opposing Blocker, i.e. pass them twice in a row, and only when the pass is earned.

questions.q: Can a Jammer score a point by passing the opposing Jammer?
questions.a: No, points can only be scored on Blockers
w: Yes, but only if they are Lead
questions.why: Points can only be scored on Blockers (including a former Jammer who became a Blocker after a Star Pass).

questions.q: On their initial trip through the Pack, how many points does a Jammer score (outside Overtime)?
questions.a: None: they must first get through the Pack and then go around the track before scoring
w: One point if they earn Lead
Four points if they come out first
questions.why: Because Jammers start behind the Pack, they must get through the Pack, then all the way around the track to be eligible to score points on opposing Blockers.

questions.q: In a normal situation, what is the maximum a Jammer can score on one scoring trip?
questions.a: Four, one per opposing Blocker
questions.why: Each team fields up to four Blockers: a scoring trip earns at most one point per opposing Blocker, so four.

questions.q: What determines that a Skater has passed another?
questions.a: Their center of mass (at the hips) moves from behind to ahead of the other Skater’s
w: Their front skates move ahead of the other’s
Their head moves ahead of the other’s
They touch the other Skater while passing
questions.why: Passing another Skater means moving so that one’s center of mass (at the hips) goes from behind to ahead of theirs, in the counterclockwise direction.

questions.q: Which of these conditions is required for a Jammer’s pass to be earned?
questions.a: Wearing the Star on their helmet, with the stars visible
w: Skating on the inside of the track
questions.why: Jammers only earn a pass if they are wearing the Star on their helmet with the stars visible, and are upright and In Bounds (or if the opponent falls back behind them).

questions.q: On a scoring trip, White Jammer passes a Red Blocker while two other Red Blockers are in the Penalty Box. How many points do they score at that moment?
questions.a: Three points
questions.why: As soon as they pass an opposing Blocker, the Jammer also passes everyone who is “Not on the Track” (NOTT), such as in the Penalty Box: 1 + 2 = 3 points.

questions.q: A team only fields three Blockers. How is the absent “fourth” Blocker treated for scoring?
questions.a: As a “Not on the Track” point: earned as soon as the Jammer passes an opposing Blocker
w: There is no point to score for that position
The point is scored automatically at the start of the Jam
The point is given to the opposing team at the end of the Jam
questions.why: Skaters who were not part of the Jam because the team did not field the maximum number of Skaters count as “Not on the Track” (NOTT).

questions.q: When does a trip through the Pack end?
questions.a: When the Jammer exits the front of the Engagement Zone
w: When they have passed all the Blockers
When they cross the Jammer Line
When the opposing Jammer enters the Pack
questions.why: A trip ends, and the next one begins, when the Jammer exits the front of the Engagement Zone (or, with No Pack, gets more than 20 feet ahead of the foremost Skater of the last defined Pack).

questions.q: On a scoring trip, White Jammer passes every Blocker except Red Pivot, who exits the front of the Engagement Zone and stays ahead. The Jammer then exits the Engagement Zone too. How many points?
questions.a: Four points
w: Three points and a penalty for the Pivot
questions.why: Leaving the front of the Engagement Zone is not a valid way to avoid being scored on: by completing their trip, the Jammer is considered to have passed the Pivot.

questions.q: How can a Blocker legally avoid being scored on?
questions.a: By staying ahead of the Jammer, or by ensuring that the pass is not earned
w: By exiting the front of the Engagement Zone
questions.why: Opponents can only avoid being scored on by staying ahead of the Jammer, or by ensuring that when they are passed, the pass is not earned.

questions.q: A Jammer is penalized but is still physically on the track. Can they still score points?
questions.a: No, they are considered no longer on the track until their penalty is complete
w: Yes, until they leave the track
Yes, until the end of their trip
Yes, if they are Lead Jammer
questions.why: A penalized Jammer is considered no longer on the track and cannot lap opponents until their penalty is complete. They then return on the same trip.

questions.q: On a scoring trip, Red Jammer passes one Blocker while removing the Star. With the Star in hand, the other three opponents go to the Penalty Box, then the Jam ends. How many points?
questions.a: One point
questions.why: The point earned while the Star was on their helmet counts. Without the Star on, they cannot score. Had they put the Star back on before the Jam ended, they would have earned the NOTT points.

questions.q: A Jammer is blocked Out of Bounds by an opponent. Do they keep earning NOTT points (Blockers in the Penalty Box, etc.)?
questions.a: Yes, when an opponent’s action is what prevents them from scoring
w: No, they score nothing while Out of Bounds
Only if they are Lead Jammer
questions.why: If an opponent’s action makes the Jammer unable to score (for example, blocked Out of Bounds), they continue to earn NOTT points as usual.

questions.q: A point was awarded in error. Until when can the score be corrected (outside the last two minutes of the game)?
questions.a: No later than the end of the Jam after the one in which the error occurred
w: Until the end of the period
Until the end of the game
Only during the Jam in which the error occurred
questions.why: The score may be corrected no later than the end of the Jam after the one in which the error occurred. With fewer than 2 minutes in the game remaining, the correction must be made before the start of that next Jam.

questions.q: Four points were correctly awarded given the information available. A review later shows the Jammer had committed a penalty two trips earlier. What happens to those points?
questions.a: They stand
w: They are given to the opposing team
questions.why: Points awarded correctly, given the information available at the time, may not be taken away later.

questions.q: On a scoring trip, the Jammer jumps the apex and passes all four Blockers while airborne. Their first skate lands In Bounds, the other then lands Out of Bounds. How many points?
questions.a: Four points
questions.why: While airborne, a Skater keeps In Bounds status if they were In Bounds before and first touch down In Bounds, and upright status if their first contact is with a skate.

questions.q: Red Jammer passes the Star to their Pivot. White Jammer, on a scoring trip, then passes all four Red Blockers, including the former Jammer. How many points?
questions.a: Four points
w: Three points, the former Jammer does not count
Zero points, the trip is voided
questions.why: All Blockers are considered tied together with respect to the opposing Jammer’s trip, including former Jammers who passed the Star.

questions.q: On a scoring trip, the Jammer has not passed anyone yet. One opposing Blocker goes to the Penalty Box, another leaves to fix their gear, then the Jam ends. How many points?
questions.a: Zero points
questions.why: The Jammer did not pass any opponent before the Jam ended. By passing the two remaining Blockers, they would also have earned the two NOTT points.

questions.q: Red Pivot has just been penalized but is still In Bounds, on their way off. White Jammer, on a scoring trip, passes them. Does this pass count?
questions.a: Yes, one point: a pass can still be earned on a penalized Blocker who is still In Bounds
w: No, a penalized Blocker no longer counts
No, and the Jammer loses that point for good
questions.why: Blockers sent to the Penalty Box but still In Bounds (or straddling) may be legally passed as if they had not been penalized.

questions.q: The Jammer passes an opponent but the pass is not earned (Star not visible). Can they still score that point?
questions.a: Yes, by yielding their position to that opponent and then passing them again legally
w: No, the point is lost for this trip
Yes, automatically at the end of the trip
questions.why: If an opponent is passed but no point is scored, the Jammer may yield their position to that opponent and re-pass them to earn the pass and score.

questions.q: White Pivot goes to the Penalty Box. Red Jammer, on a scoring trip, passes two White Blockers before the Pivot returns and the Jam ends. How many points?
questions.a: Three points
questions.why: By passing the first Blocker while the Pivot was in the Penalty Box, the Jammer also earned the NOTT point on the Pivot: 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: How long is a penalty?
questions.a: 30 seconds of Jam time
w: Until the end of the current Jam
questions.why: Skaters serve 30 seconds of Jam time for each penalty. Penalties are only timed while a Jam is in progress.

questions.q: Which part of a penalty must be served standing?
questions.a: The final 10 seconds
questions.why: The final 10 seconds of penalty time must be served while standing.

questions.q: When does penalty time begin?
questions.a: As soon as the Skater sits in the Penalty Box, in any seat
w: As soon as the penalty is called
As soon as the Skater leaves the track
At the start of the next Jam
questions.why: Upon sitting in any seat in the Penalty Box, the Skater’s penalty time begins (see also Scenario C4.4.1.A).

questions.q: A Skater stands too early in the Penalty Box. What happens?
questions.a: Their time stops until they are seated again
w: Their time is reset to zero
questions.why: If a Skater stands early, their time stops until they are seated again.

questions.q: A Skater sits in the Penalty Box between Jams. When does their penalty time begin?
questions.a: At the start of the following Jam
w: At the end of the Lineup Time
questions.why: Penalties are only timed while a Jam is in progress. Timing for Skaters who sit between Jams does not begin until the start of the following Jam.

questions.q: How many Blockers from the same team can be seated in the Penalty Box at the same time?
questions.a: Two
questions.why: At most two Blockers per team may be seated in the Penalty Box at the same time.

questions.q: A third Blocker arrives at the Penalty Box while two Blockers from their team are seated. What happens?
questions.a: They are placed “In Queue” and must return to play until a seat opens
w: They wait standing next to the Penalty Box
They take the seat of whoever arrived first
They are removed from the Jam
questions.why: The third Blocker is In Queue and must return to play. They come back to the Penalty Box when a seat opens (unless that would destroy the Pack) or when instructed by an Official.

questions.q: Two Red Blockers are in the Penalty Box and one is already standing for their final 10 seconds. A third Red Blocker arrives. Can they sit?
questions.a: Yes, in the open seat
w: No, they must wait for the Penalty Box to empty
No, they are placed In Queue
Yes, but their time only starts in the next Jam
questions.why: If a Blocker is standing in the Penalty Box, another Blocker may sit in the open seat.

questions.q: White Jammer has served 25 seconds when Red Jammer sits in the Penalty Box. What happens?
questions.a: White is released immediately, and Red serves 25 seconds
w: White serves their last 5 seconds, then Red serves 30
questions.why: The two Jammers serve as little time as possible, an equivalent amount per penalty, with one Jammer not serving a penalty whenever possible. The first is released as soon as the other sits.

questions.q: Both Jammers sit in the Penalty Box at exactly the same moment during a Jam. What happens?
questions.a: Both are released immediately
w: The Jammer who arrived first serves 30 seconds
questions.why: If both Jammers sit simultaneously, they will both be released immediately.

questions.q: Red Jammer is in the Penalty Box. White Jammer sits down between Jams. When is Red released?
questions.a: At the start of the next Jam
w: After 30 seconds of the next Jam
They are not released, both serve their time
questions.why: If one Jammer sits between Jams, the other Jammer should be released at the start of the next Jam.

questions.q: The opposing Jammer is absent (equipment malfunction) when a Jammer is sent to the Penalty Box. What happens?
questions.a: The Jam ends once the penalized Jammer is seated
w: The Jam continues with no Jammer
The Pivot automatically becomes the Jammer
questions.why: If a Jammer is sent to the Box when there is no opposing Jammer, the Jam will end once the Jammer is seated. This ensures that there is one Jammer who is not serving a penalty.

questions.q: How many penalties make a Skater foul out of the game?
questions.a: Seven
questions.why: When seven penalties are recorded for a Skater, that Skater fouls out of the game, including penalties assessed on behalf of their team.

questions.q: Who has the authority to expel a Skater, coach or other Team Staff?
questions.a: Only the Head Referee
questions.why: The Head Referee is the only Official with the authority to expel. Other Officials may recommend expulsions to the Head Referee.

questions.q: A Skater is expelled. Who serves their penalty?
questions.a: A substitute
w: The Captain, on top of their own penalties
The team plays one short until the end of the period
questions.why: A substitute must serve the penalty for an expelled Skater. If a Non-Skater is expelled, the team’s Captain serves the penalty, but it is not recorded against them.

questions.q: Which protective gear may be removed in the Penalty Box?
questions.a: Only the mouthguard, which must be put back before leaving the Penalty Box
questions.why: Skaters may remove their mouthguard, but no other protective gear. They must put it back before leaving the Penalty Box (or be penalized).

questions.q: What does “cutting the track” mean?
questions.a: Using the area out of bounds to gain position on someone who is upright and In Bounds
w: Crossing the infield to reach the Penalty Box
Passing on the inside in a turn
questions.why: It is illegal to use the area outside the track boundaries to gain position on someone who is upright and In Bounds.

questions.q: A Skater was blocked off the track by an opponent while they were ahead of that opponent. Where must they return?
questions.a: Behind that opponent, even if they were ahead before the block
w: To the position they held before the block
Anywhere, since an opponent knocked them out
questions.why: If a Skater goes out of bounds due to an opponent’s block, they must return behind that opponent, unless that opponent goes Down, Out of Bounds or Out of Play in the meantime.

questions.q: Returning to the track, a Jammer cuts in front of just one of their own teammates. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: cutting a single teammate does not have sufficient impact
questions.why: Cutting a single teammate does not have enough impact to warrant a penalty. Cutting more than one teammate is penalized.

questions.q: A Skater has illegally re-entered the track. How can they cede the advantage without a penalty?
questions.a: By immediately returning fully Out of Bounds, before re-entering
w: By straddling the boundary for a few seconds
By slowing down on the track
questions.why: To cede, the Skater must immediately return fully Out of Bounds before re-entering. Straddling the track boundary is not sufficient.

questions.q: White Pivot is Down, In Bounds. Red Pivot dodges them by going Out of Bounds, then re-enters ahead of them after they get up. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty: a Down Skater does not hold superior position
questions.why: Down Skaters do not hold superior position over Skaters who are Out of Bounds.

questions.q: Out of Bounds, a Jammer accelerates counterclockwise outside the track to stay ahead of the Pack before re-entering. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty
w: No penalty, they are Out of Bounds
No penalty if they re-enter behind whoever knocked them out
questions.why: Skaters may not accelerate or maintain speed while out of bounds, except to return to the track sooner or to reach the Penalty Box faster. Clockwise movement is not penalized.

questions.q: After being penalized, where must a Skater leave the track?
questions.a: To the outside, near where the penalty was called
w: By the shortest route to the Penalty Box, even across the infield
questions.why: After a penalty, the Skater must exit the track to the outside, near where it was called (they may briefly go through the infield for safety reasons, see C4.4.B).

questions.q: Where must a Skater who left the track legally (to go to the Penalty Box or fix their gear) re-enter?
questions.a: Behind all in-play Blockers
w: At the exact spot where they left
questions.why: Skaters who intentionally but legally leave the track must re-enter behind all in-play Blockers (or, with No Pack, behind those within 20 feet of the last defined Pack), without illegally gaining position.

questions.q: A Jammer stands at 20 seconds, looks at the scoreboard and leaves the Penalty Box without anyone releasing them. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty if they fully leave the Penalty Box early, even by a fraction of a second
w: No penalty if their time is almost up
They only have to come back and finish their time
questions.why: Leaving the Penalty Box early without good reason is always penalized. Had an Official told them their time was up, they would have had good reason to leave.

questions.q: Who may enter the Penalty Box?
questions.a: Only Officials and Skaters serving penalties
w: Coaches, to talk to their Skaters
questions.why: Nobody may enter the Penalty Box except for Officials and Skaters who are serving penalties.

questions.q: A team that has already used its three Team Timeouts calls a fourth, which is granted in error. It still has its Official Review. What happens?
questions.a: The team is considered to have used its Official Review as a timeout
w: The timeout is cancelled with no consequence
questions.why: If the team still has an Official Review, it is considered used as a timeout. Otherwise the Captain is penalized. Officials should normally decline the request, without a penalty.

questions.q: As the Lineup Time expires, a team has four Blockers correctly positioned but its Jammer is still Out of Bounds. What should the Officials do?
questions.a: Call an Official Timeout instead of starting the Jam, and penalize that team’s Captain
w: Start the Jam with no Jammer for that team
Wait until the Jammer is ready, no penalty
questions.why: The team failed to field a correctly positioned Jammer, which prevents the Jam from starting: Official Timeout and a penalty to the Captain.

questions.q: The Captain, who is not visibly wearing a “C”, signals for a Team Timeout. What happens?
questions.a: The Team Timeout is granted, and the Captain is penalized
w: The Team Timeout is granted with no penalty
The Team Timeout is refused and the Captain is penalized
questions.why: Even without a visible “C”, the Captain keeps the privilege of calling a Team Timeout, but exercising it without the letter visible warrants a penalty.

questions.q: An off-skates team member (coach, staff) commits a penalty. Who receives it?
questions.a: The team’s Captain
w: The Pivot of the current Jam
questions.why: If off-skates Team Staff commit a penalty, the penalty should be assessed to the appropriate team’s Captain.

questions.q: The Captain receives a penalty as Captain (on behalf of the team). When do they serve it?
questions.a: In the next Jam in which they are able to serve as a Blocker
w: Immediately, even if they are on the bench
At the end of the period
They do not serve it, it is only recorded
questions.why: If a penalty is assessed to a Captain because they are the Captain, they serve it in the next Jam in which they are able to serve as a Blocker (see C5.4.A).

questions.q: A team’s only Blocker on the track commits a penalty. What happens?
questions.a: They are not sent off the track until another Blocker from their team rejoins the Pack
w: They leave for the Penalty Box immediately
The penalty is given to the Captain
questions.why: If the only Blocker from a team on the track commits a penalty, they should not be sent off the track until another Blocker from their team rejoins the Pack.

questions.q: White Pivot arrives at the Penalty Box between Jams and says they are injured. What happens?
questions.a: A substitute serves the penalty in the same Role, and the Pivot may not skate for the next three Jams
w: The Pivot must serve their penalty anyway
The team plays one short for 30 seconds
questions.why: A substitute may serve the penalty of a Skater unable to do so (injury, broken equipment) once the Jam is over. The replaced Skater may not participate in the following three Jams.

questions.q: A Blocker is assessed a penalty and swears loudly enough for the audience to hear. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty
questions.why: Obscene language audible to the audience or broadcast is penalized, as are insults directed at an Official. A few words to a teammate or opponent warrant a warning first.

questions.q: An Official overhears a Skater making racist, sexist, homophobic or transphobic remarks. What is the call?
questions.a: Expulsion
w: No sanction during play, only after the game
questions.why: Abusive behavior (hateful, prejudiced or bigoted remarks…) results in an expulsion. Organizers may take further action outside the game.

questions.q: Coming back from the Penalty Box, a Blocker pushes a referee with their forearm to keep their path. What is the call?
questions.a: Expulsion
w: No penalty, the referee was in their way
questions.why: Forceful, avoidable or negligent contact with an Official is unsporting and always warrants an expulsion.

questions.q: A Blocker intentionally pulls the Star off the opposing Jammer’s helmet. What is the call?
questions.a: The Blocker is expelled
w: No penalty, but the Jammer keeps Lead
questions.why: Intentionally removing an opponent’s helmet cover is serious unsporting conduct, resulting in an expulsion. The Jammer temporarily loses the ability to score or earn Lead.

questions.q: In the Penalty Box, a White Blocker imitates an Official by saying “Red, [number], done”. Red Jammer leaves, thinking they were released. What is the call?
questions.a: Penalty for White; Red is not penalized but must come back to finish their time
w: Penalty for Red, for leaving early
questions.why: Imitating an Official’s instructions to cause an opponent’s penalty is unsporting. Red acted in good faith but must serve the rest of their penalty.

questions.q: During a Jam, a mouthguard lies on the track and no Skater makes an immediate attempt to retrieve it. What happens?
questions.a: The Jam is called off and the Skater missing their mouthguard is penalized
w: Play continues, an Official picks it up
The Skater must leave until the end of the Jam, no penalty
questions.why: The mouthguard is required protective gear. If it is not immediately put back, the Jam is called off and a penalty is assessed.

questions.q: Should a penalty be assessed for an illegal action that has little or no impact on the game?
questions.a: No, penalties are not assessed for actions without sufficient impact
w: Yes, every illegal action is penalized
Only if the opponent asks for it
questions.why: Penalties should not be assessed for actions that have little or no impact on the game or on the Skaters.

questions.q: During the Lineup Time, a team intentionally puts eight Blockers and two Jammers on the track, then sends some off at the five-second call. What happens?
questions.a: Official Timeout and an Unsporting Conduct penalty to the Captain
w: Nothing, as long as they leave before the start
A penalty for each extra Skater
The Jam starts and the extra Skaters are penalized
questions.why: Intentionally fielding more Skaters than allowed is unsporting: it impacts the opponents’ starting position and strategy.

questions.q: By mistake, a team fields one Blocker too many. An Official notices after the start and sends them off before their presence has any impact. What is the call?
questions.a: No penalty
w: The Jam is stopped and replayed
questions.why: The extra Blocker left play before having any impact. Had they stayed, the Officials should have called off the Jam and assessed a penalty.

questions.q: A Blocker hears their penalty but keeps blocking the opposing Jammer to let their teammates reposition, then leaves. What is the call?
questions.a: An additional penalty for not leaving the track immediately
w: Their penalty is simply extended by 10 seconds
questions.why: Once a penalty is called, the Skater must immediately leave the track. Deliberately continuing to play gives an advantage and is penalized.

questions.q: Who is the ultimate authority for the game?
questions.a: The Head Referee
questions.why: One Referee is designated as Head Referee: they are the ultimate authority for the game.

questions.q: What must Referees who assess and enforce penalties do?
questions.a: Be on skates and wear a uniform that clearly identifies them
w: Sit by the side of the track
Be at least four per game
questions.why: Referees must be on skates and wear a uniform that clearly identifies them. They must also be distinguishable from one another (name or number).

questions.q: An Official is not certain that an action warrants a penalty. What should they do?
questions.a: Not assess a penalty
w: Assess the penalty just in case
questions.why: No penalty should be assessed unless the Official is certain that it is warranted. If Officials disagree, the Head Referee’s decision is final.

questions.q: During a Jam, a penalty is warranted but it is unclear which Skater on the team is responsible. Who receives it?
questions.a: The nearest Blocker from that team
questions.why: Mid-Jam, the penalty goes to the nearest Blocker from the appropriate team; between Jams, to the Captain. If the responsible team is uncertain, no penalty is assessed.

questions.q: A Penalty Box Official releases a Skater too early. They return to play. Are they penalized?
questions.a: No, Skaters are not penalized for actions based on incorrect information from an Official
w: Yes, for leaving the Penalty Box early
Yes, but only with a warning
Yes, if the opposing team reports it
questions.why: If an Official provides incorrect information, the Skater is not penalized for actions taken on that basis. Failing to provide information (e.g. no warning) is not an error, however.

questions.q: Their Jammer Referee wrongly signals to a Jammer that they are Lead. The Jammer calls off the Jam. Are they penalized?
questions.a: No
w: Yes, for illegally calling off the Jam
Yes, and their team loses the Jam’s points
questions.why: A Jammer who calls off a Jam while their Jammer Referee indicates they are Lead is not penalized, even if they did not actually have Lead.

questions.q: From when must a Skater behave as penalized?
questions.a: Once the Official has called the penalty with the correct hand signal and verbal cue
w: As soon as they think they committed a foul
As soon as the opposing team protests
At the end of the Jam
questions.why: Penalties must be assessed at a volume sufficient to be heard; until this has occurred, nobody is required to behave as if the Skater has been penalized.

questions.q: Can Officials call off a Jam at their discretion?
questions.a: Yes, for example for an injury, a technical difficulty or unsafe play
w: No, only the Lead Jammer can call off a Jam
No, only the clock can end it
Only at the end of a period
questions.why: Officials may call off Jams at their discretion: injuries, technical difficulties, interference, unsafe play, or illegal play that cannot be remedied with a penalty.

questions.q: Can Non-Skating Officials (NSOs) assess penalties?
questions.a: Yes, those relevant to their role in the game, unless prohibited by the Head Referee
questions.why: Non-Skating Officials may assess penalties that are relevant to their role as an official in the game, unless prohibited from doing so by the Head Referee.

questions.q: A Skater repeatedly proves to be a significant danger on the track, without any foul warranting an expulsion. What can the Head Referee do?
questions.a: Remove them from play at their discretion, without having to expel them
w: Nothing, as long as there is no foul
questions.why: The Head Referee oversees safety and may use their discretion to remove a dangerous Skater from play, without the need for an expulsion.

questions.q: A Blocker has reason to believe they are in play, but they are Out of Play. Can they be penalized for this technical infraction?
questions.a: Only after receiving a warning
w: Only if they block the Jammer
questions.why: Skaters who have reason to believe they are in play should not be penalized for technical Out of Play infractions, unless a warning has been given.

questions.q: A Skater has their skates on the track and touches the floor outside only with one hand. Are they In Bounds?
questions.a: Yes, touching outside with only one arm or hand does not count
w: No, they are Out of Bounds
Only if their hand is on the line
questions.why: A Skater who touches the floor beyond the track boundary with only one arm or hand is still considered In Bounds.

questions.q: A Skater has one skate on the track and one skate beyond the boundary. How are they considered (unless otherwise noted)?
questions.a: Out of Bounds (they are straddling)
questions.why: A Skater is straddling when touching the floor both in bounds and beyond the track boundary. Straddling Skaters are considered Out of Bounds, except where otherwise noted.

questions.q: A Skater is crouching with just one hand on the floor. Are they “Down”?
questions.a: No, if their only contact with the floor besides their skates is one hand
w: Yes, as soon as a hand touches the floor
Only if they are Out of Bounds
questions.why: A Skater is Down when part of their body or equipment (aside from skates) touches the floor. If that only contact is one hand, they are not Down.

questions.q: What does “immediately” mean in the rules?
questions.a: At the first safe and legal opportunity to take the action
w: Before the end of the Jam
questions.why: “Immediately” means the first safe and legal opportunity during which a person can undertake an action.

questions.q: What is the maximum length of the Lineup Time between two Jams?
questions.a: 30 seconds
questions.why: Lineup Time is the time during which the period clock runs between the end of one Jam and either the start of the next Jam (at most 30 seconds) or a timeout.

questions.q: Which protective gear must Skaters wear?
questions.a: Helmet, mouthguard, wrist guards, elbow pads and knee pads
questions.why: Skaters must wear a helmet, mouthguard, wrist guards, elbow pads and knee pads.
